title: Earth Observation Sentinel
description: Design a high-yield Earth observation satellite to monitor climate patterns, deforestation, and atmospheric dynamics. Must ensure reliable downlink to ground stations during frequent ground passes.
objectives: Ensure sufficient electrical power during orbital eclipse phases
Deploy multispectral cameras and spectrometers for environmental monitoring
Maintain downlink throughput above data generation rate
scientificGoals: Generate high-resolution surface maps with minimal data loss
Measure atmospheric CO2 and aerosol optical depth
Survive 2 years of continuous orbital thermal cycling
environmentalChallenges: Frequent eclipse shadow periods requiring steady battery capacity
High atmospheric drag at lower orbital altitudes
Rapid ground station contact windows (10-15 min per pass)
educationalNotes: Earth orbit missions benefit from full 1.0 AU solar flux (1361 W/m²), but pass through Earth's shadow every 90 minutes. Adequate battery capacity is mandatory.

title: Lunar Water-Ice Mapper
description: Chart permanently shadowed craters at the lunar south pole to locate volatile water-ice deposits critical for future Artemis base camps. Must balance mass, power, and high-frequency radar sounding.
objectives: Execute lunar insertion burn with positive delta-V margin
Deploy laser altimeter and radar sounder to detect subsurface volatiles
Maintain telemetry link with NASA Deep Space Network stations
Ensure structural hull survives cislunar transit and micrometeorite fluxes
scientificGoals: Map south pole crater depths down to 1-meter vertical accuracy
Identify subsurface hydrogen signatures via neutron/radar spectroscopy
Establish gravity gradient anomalies for future lunar landings
environmentalChallenges: Extreme thermal gradients (+120°C in sunlight to -230°C in shadowed craters)
Solar wind particle bombardment outside Earth's magnetosphere
Lunar mass concentrations (mascons) perturbing low orbits
educationalNotes: The Moon has no atmosphere and sits outside Earth's protective magnetic field. Radiation and thermal control become primary engineering drivers.

title: Mars Climate & Atmospheric Orbiter
description: Investigate the red planet's atmospheric loss mechanisms, historical climate shifts, and seasonal dust storm dynamics. Demands efficient propulsion for interplanetary transit and communications across up to 20 light-minutes.
objectives: Calculate and survive Mars orbital capture delta-V
Compensate for reduced solar flux at 1.52 AU (43% of Earth's solar intensity)
Downlink high-definition hyperspectral data with realistic light-time delays
Survive solar particle events during cruise phase
scientificGoals: Track atmospheric escape rates of hydrogen and oxygen ions
Characterize seasonal polar cap sublimation and ice inventory
Locate potential past aqueous habitability zones
environmentalChallenges: Solar irradiance drops to 590 W/m² (requires larger solar arrays or RTG)
Round-trip communication delay between 6 and 44 minutes prevents real-time teleoperation
Deep space radiation during the 7-month cruise phase
educationalNotes: Because Mars orbits at 1.52 AU, solar flux drops by 1/r² = 1/(1.52)² ≈ 43%. A solar panel that outputs 1000W at Earth will only yield 433W at Mars!

title: Europa Life Search & Ocean Explorer
description: Humanity's most audacious outer-solar mission: Probe Jupiter's moon Europa to determine if its subsurface saltwater ocean harbors conditions suitable for extraterrestrial life. Extreme radiation and extreme distance test every engineering subsystem.
objectives: Comply with strict $500M budget and 2,000 kg total spacecraft mass limits
Survive lethal trapped radiation belts around Jupiter (thousands of times Earth levels)
Provide steady baseload power at 5.2 AU where sunlight is only 3.7% of Earth's
Deploy ice-penetrating radar to measure ice shell thickness above the liquid ocean
scientificGoals: Sound through the 15-25 km ice crust to detect liquid water interfaces
Search for active vapor plumes and organic biosignature molecules
Measure induced magnetic dipole confirming global saline ocean conductivity
environmentalChallenges: Sunlight is only 3.7% (1/5.2² = 0.037) of Earth flux: solar panels become massive and ineffective
Jupiter's intense magnetosphere bombards spacecraft with relativistic electrons (>100 krad)
Light delay exceeds 40 minutes each way; autonomous fault response is critical
Mass limit of 2,000 kg requires extreme optimization between shielding, instruments, and fuel
educationalNotes: Europa is the ultimate engineering crucible. Solar arrays require massive area (like Europa Clipper's 30-meter wings) or heavy, costly RTGs. Radiation shielding is non-negotiable.
